en: Compiled by Śramaṇa Jizang.
Chapter Ten: Refuting Emptiness (Part Two of the Lower Section).
This tenth chapter, "Refuting Emptiness," is not only the profound ultimate principle of this treatise, but is also the very heart-essence of the Vaipulya sūtras. It says:
Concise yet its meaning is manifest;
elegant in expression yet leading to profound depth.
When applied with rectitude, there is nothing correct that it cannot penetrate.
If one employs it to crush heterodoxy, then heterodoxy will not fail to submit;
it can subdue celestial Māras, restrain non-Buddhists, refute the Lesser Vehicle, and blunt grandiose views.
If one relies upon it to strike down delusions, then all burdens of affliction will be leveled.
To employ it in practicing the Way means that contemplation will leave nothing unilluminated;
it can awaken the wisdom of the ignorant and give rise to the eloquence of the stammering.
It is truly the essential method for regulating the mind and the clear art of purification through repentance.
When I was still a youth, I studied these subtle and profound mysteries;
as I approached the age of sixty, I took them up as a mirror for my mind.
However, as my notes have fallen into disarray, I now preserve only their general outline.
The intent of this work differs [from others], and its ten meanings are briefly elucidated as follows.
First, if it is divided according to three sections:
the first chapter, "Refuting the Self," clarifies the emptiness of sentient beings.
Having already refuted [the notion of] permanence and subsequently established the emptiness of all phenomena,
this present chapter clarifies that even the "sickness" of emptiness is empty.
Vimalakīrti employs these three gates as a method for disciplining the mind.
Therefore, I have briefly elucidated this previously;
Deva also takes these three as the method for refining the spirit,
which he will explain extensively hereafter.
Second, if divided into two sections, there are two types of relinquishment:

first, the relinquishment of transgressions; second, the relinquishment of merit. This consists of: one, explaining the relinquishment of transgressions; and two, distinguishing the relinquishment of merit.
Refuting heterodoxy also has two aspects:
first, refuting the view of existence; second, refuting the view of emptiness.
From [the refutation of] the "Self" (ātman) up to [the refutation of] "eternalism," these refute the view of existence.
Now, this chapter successively refutes the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*).
Existence and non-existence are the root of all views and the foundation of obstacles to the Middle Way;
therefore, they must be refuted.
Thus, when the roots of all views are overturned, the reality within them is revealed.
Third, regarding the division between that which can refute and that which is to be refuted:
from the very beginning of this treatise, it has refuted that which is to be refuted.
Now, in this chapter, we shall next refute the refuter itself.
When both the refuter and the refuted are leveled and both the refutation and the establishment are extinguished, then all is suddenly void and without basis.
The phenomena do not lose their reality, yet they are serene and beyond reliance.
The principle naturally converges in mystery.
Fourth, if one examines and analyzes it from the perspective of conditions (*pratyaya*),
what has been explained above clarifies that conditions are exhausted within contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Now, this chapter clarifies that contemplation culminates in conditions,
and conditions culminate in contemplation.

This means that whether it be transgression or merit, phenomena or persons, birth-and-death or nirvana, ordinary beings or sages, delusion or awakening— there is no source from which these can be sought.
Because the contemplation is exhausted within [the object], it is called "contemplation that exhausts the object.
Regarding "the contemplation exhausting the object":
once the object has been exhausted, the correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) then ceases.
When conditions are exhausted within contemplation, there is no longer conditioning;
when contemplation is exhausted within conditions, there is no longer contemplation.
Therefore, it is neither condition nor contemplation.
I do not know how to name it; I have tentatively called it "Right Contemplation," and it is also provisionally designated as "Prajñā," "Buddha-nature," and "Dharmakāya."
Therefore, they are designated according to their respective meanings. For example,
what is called *prajñā* is a single dharma that the Buddha has taught under various names.
According to the capacities of sentient beings, he establishes different characters for them.
Fifth is the clarification of guest and host.
From the refutation of the self (*ātman*) up to the refutation of permanence, these are the propositions established by the non-Buddhists as Deva argues the case.
This chapter elucidates the debates on the tenets of the Tīrthikas by Deva.
When the Tīrthikas establish their propositions and Deva refutes them with his own arguments,
there is no difficulty he does not crush, and no point of penetration he does not subdue.
When Deva elucidated his own school’s tenets and debated with the non-Buddhists,
there was no objection that he did not answer, and no answer that did not refute [the opponent].
The reason for this was as follows:
The non-Buddhists do not rely upon emptiness in their questions and answers;
therefore, their questions fail to be valid questions and their answers fail to be valid answers.
Since the Master of the Treatise relies upon emptiness in his questioning, there is no objection that cannot be demolished.
By responding based on emptiness, there is no answer that does not resolve the inquiry.
This is shown to sentient beings of the final age to clarify that even mundane questions and answers must rely upon emptiness.
How much more so for one who wishes to leave suffering behind and seek the path to quiescence—how could such a person persist in clinging to existence?
Sixth, from the preceding sections onward is called "Refuting the Erroneous" (poxie);
this present chapter is titled "Refuting the Correct" (pozheng).
However, it is because there is internal correctness in contrast to the heterodoxy of external paths that such correctness exists.
Since heterodoxy cannot be established, correctness likewise does not remain.
This is similarly true for the meanings of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, truth and falsehood, as well as what lies outside and within the principle, including the concepts of attainment and non-attainment.
Śākyamuni’s single period [of teaching] was likewise thus:
from the beginning at the Deer Park, he pursued the various non-Buddhists until his arrival at the Twin Śāla Trees, where the heterodox paths of the Six Teachers were utterly extinguished.
The orthodoxy of Śākyamuni has likewise ceased; Deva was the same.
Thus, having previously excluded external heterodoxy, one now brings internal orthodoxy to rest.
Just as when Duke Hu’s medicine was hidden, Duke Hu himself was also concealed; the matter here is likewise.
Seventh: whereas the preceding sections refuted various masters individually, this chapter refutes all non-Buddhist schools (tīrthikas) collectively.
Eighth, discussing this in terms of persons:
previously, the views of the non-Buddhists who hold to existence were refuted; now, the views of the non-Buddhists who hold to emptiness are refuted.
Previously, the Sarvāstivādins were refuted; now, the Vaipulya school is refuted.
The former refuted those with an excess of craving; now, it refutes those with an excess of views.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Those with an excess of craving cling to existence; those with an excess of views cling to emptiness."
Ninth: What has been presented above was the correct refutation of the non-Buddhists;
this present chapter is titled "The Explanation of the Refutation.
As for "the explanation of the refutation," it refers to the refutation of false views.
It is called "breaking" (*po*) because it halts at the perception of water;
it is called "explaining the breaking" (*shi-po*) because there is actually no water to be broken.
Tenth, whereas the preceding sections constituted the direct refutation (*zheng-po*), this present chapter is named the "discriminating refutation" (*jian-po*).
The reason for this is that even among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders there are mutual refutations,
and even among the five hundred masters of the Hinayana there are mutual refutations.
Even among those who have attained the Mahāyāna, there are mutual refutations;
yet, the one with superior intellectual power triumphs, while the one with inferior intellectual power suffers defeat.
Now, Āryadeva likewise refutes the non-Buddhists, distinguishing himself from their various teachers.
The various masters all have something attained in their minds and something upon which they dwell in their speech;
for this reason, they refute others.
Deva has nothing upon which his mind relies and nothing upon which his speech dwells.
Therefore, it is neither a refutation nor a non-refutation;
rather, it is called a "refutation" because one falsely claims that something exists when it cannot be found upon investigation.
Because there was in fact nothing to be refuted,
he differed from those various masters. In the fourth year of the Daye era, in order to confront the three types of masters of the treatises in Chang’an—

namely, the masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Daśabhūmika*, and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*— he took the elucidation of the principle of the two kinds of selflessness and the three natures as the main body of his discourse.
This present chapter is established precisely to refute that [position];
it should be titled "The Chapter Refuting the Two Kinds of Selflessness" and "The Chapter Refuting the Three Natures.
How is this known?

The principle of the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena has been explained; the refutation of the "one" and so forth concludes the clarification of the principle of the selflessness of phenomena.
Now, to speak of "refuting emptiness" means to refute both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena.
Is this not the refutation of the principle of the two kinds of selflessness?
This is simply the nature of Āryadeva himself;
do not blame the lecturer.
Regarding the statement "Refuting the Chapter on the Principle of the Three Non-natures":
you take saṃsāra, the objects, and consciousness as the two natures of the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*),
and take nirvāṇa as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The above has completed the refutation of these three natures.
Now, furthermore, emptiness is being refuted;
is this not, indeed, the refutation of the three non-natures?
This is also the Master of the Treatise’s own clarification;
it was not arbitrarily fabricated by another.
Question: What is it that [the author] intends to clarify by refuting both the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)?
The response is: "Is it that I lack a self-nature or the nature of non-existence?
These five propositions may be understood by oneself.
Furthermore, to provide the introductory context for the arrival of this chapter:
This not only consolidates the intent behind Deva’s single-period appearance in the world,
but also reaffirms the intent behind Nāgārjuna’s appearance as a śāstra-master.
This is because people who lecture on Nāgārjuna’s Four Treatises fail to understand the true meaning of those treatises.
Therefore, after Deva had finished refuting the non-Buddhists, he further composed this treatise to clarify the intent behind Nāgārjuna’s appearance in the world to refute and explain [the truth].
Having thus recounted Deva’s appearance in the world and the intent of Nāgārjuna, [he proceeds as follows].
This is the general purport concerning Śākyamuni’s single lifetime as well as all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Furthermore, regarding the purpose for which this chapter is presented: it clarifies the meaning of the correct teaching on the resolution of delusion and the attainment of understanding.
All followers of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna say that one severs delusions through the realization of emptiness; thus,
the delusions are the objects to be severed, while the realization of emptiness is the means by which they are severed.
Therefore, there is the refutation through the realization of unimpeded right abandonment and liberation;
furthermore, there is the refutation through the obstruction of unimpeded right penetration and liberation.
This continues until it is said that the Buddha’s wisdom abandons the hindrances.
Therefore, this present chapter is established to clarify that there is neither establishment nor refutation;
it clarifies that there are no delusions to be severed. Since there are no delusions to sever, what capacity for understanding could there be to refute them?
Therefore, this chapter is taught.
Furthermore, it clarifies the intent of repentance according to the various Vaipulya sutras.
People of the world all say:
"I now wish to repent for the multitude of sins committed since beginningless time.
In this context, one regards the sin as that which is to be destroyed and the repentance as that which destroys it;
such repentance is termed "repentance of transgressions."
How is this known? Since those who are capable of refuting and that which is to be refuted are both non-Buddhists,
how can it now be said that there is repentance as the refuter and sin as that which is to be refuted?
"Is this not the teaching of non-Buddhists?
These words are truly meant only for those who have entered into the principle.
Thus spoke the Great Master of the Mountains in the past.
One must not allow people to speak after leaving the lecture hall;
the intention lies precisely here.
It is because one fears that if they hear [the teaching], they might give rise to doubt and slander.
Furthermore, regarding the introduction to this chapter:
it is intended to explain the meaning of the intrinsic purity and non-arising/non-ceasing of all Mahāyāna sūtras.
As for what is called "non-arising":
Fundamentally there is no arising of persons, and fundamentally there is no arising of dharmas.
How could there be establishment?
Ultimately, there is no cessation.
What is it that is negated?
Therefore, the non-establishment of negation is precisely the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, it explains that in the various Vaipulya sutras, one does not sever the afflictions, yet one does not dwell together with them either.
Because they are not established, they do not coexist;
because there is nothing to be refuted, there is no cessation.
All such categories of meaning should be understood in this way.
In the past, when Jizang was in Jiangzuo, he presented this chapter as consisting of seventeen sections;
however, due to his advanced age and frequent forgetfulness, he has here briefly recounted only one or two of them.
As for what is called the "Chapter on the Refutation of Emptiness" (Pòkōng pǐn), there are generally two meanings.
First, various non-Buddhists and others cling to the myriad transformations as being existent;
yet when they seek their ultimate source, they find nothing.
Consequently, by asserting that both persons and phenomena are empty, they fall into the view of nihilism.
Now, because it refutes the arbitrary claims of outsiders that [all things] are empty, it is called "Refuting Emptiness.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Sentient beings give rise to views in two general ways."
First is annihilationism and second is eternalism.
Furthermore, it is said that these must be based on annihilationism and eternalism.
The reason for this is as follows:
One must first give rise to the view of permanence by means of the causes that give rise to the view of annihilationism.
Second, the Master of the Treatise clarifies in the first chapter that one abandons sin by relying on merit, and abandons merit by relying on emptiness.

From the refutation of the self (*ātman*) onward, he proceeds to refute the permanent [self], seeking the non-existence of persons and phenomena, thereby explaining and establishing the meaning of emptiness.
Once the meaning of emptiness is established, the relinquishing of merit becomes manifest.
If those of sharp faculties among the non-Buddhists enter the right path through this gateway of emptiness,
those of dull faculties, however, become further attached to emptiness itself.
In that case, emptiness would not be a gateway.
Now, because this chapter refutes this [notion of] emptiness to enable awakening and entry, it is called "refuting emptiness.
Question: Emptiness is a non-existent dharma.
"What is it that is being destroyed?
Thus, the non-Buddhists rebuked Deva, saying:
"It is like a foolish person who wishes to destroy empty space; there is only the fault of fruitless labor."
For what reason do you now say that emptiness is being refuted?
Answer: It is said that emptiness is refuted because one refutes the sickness of clinging to emptiness;
in reality, there is no emptiness to be refuted.
Question: If that is so, one should have titled it "Chapter on Refuting Illness" (Pó bìng pǐn) rather than "Chapter on Refuting Emptiness" (Pó kōng pǐn).
Answer: Illness is the subject that grasps, while emptiness is the object that is grasped.
If one were to call it "Chapter on Refuting Illness," then all ten chapters would be refutations of illness.
Now, because this chapter reveals the defects of the grasping subject by means of the emptiness that is being upheld, it is titled "The Chapter on Refuting Emptiness" (*Pó kōng pǐn*).
Question: The Master of the Treatise has previously refuted the existence of external objects; since the outsiders have been defeated, [what remains?]
Now, regarding this chapter on the outsider Nāgārjuna’s critique of emptiness:
why was Nāgārjuna able to master it?
The answer is that the outsiders possessed [theories of] existence that could be refuted.
For this reason, he accepts his defeat;
the master of the treatise has nothing to be reproached for,
and thus remains serene and detached.
Question: Does this chapter merely refute emptiness, or does it also refute the four propositions?
Answer: It refutes all four propositions regarding emptiness;
however, because the preceding eight chapters refuted existence, this chapter clarifies the refutation of emptiness.
Furthermore, there is emptiness that exists, existence that exists, that which is both empty and existent, and that which is neither empty nor existent—
all of these are termed "existence.
Only when these four propositions are absent is it called "emptiness."
The refutation of emptiness in this treatise means that all four positions, both internal and external, are completely refuted.
Question: If all four positions, internal and external, are completely refuted, then there should be nothing to be established.
Answer: To refute these various internal and external views is precisely to awaken to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
this is what constitutes "expounding" (*shen*).
Question: If that is so, one would only be expounding the true reality and not expounding the gates of the teachings (*śāsana-mukha*).
Answer: The teaching fundamentally elucidates the principle (*tattva*).
Once one has already seen the moon, what need is there for the finger?
Question: If that were so, one would subsequently fail to understand the two truths (*satyadvaya*).
Answer: For one who has attained realization, there is likewise no need for the two truths.
Furthermore, the four positions of the non-Buddhists have been refuted above without exception;
only when the obstructions are first removed can the two truths be clearly elucidated.
This chapter is divided into two parts:
first, the refutation of the nihilistic emptiness of the non-Buddhists;
second, the presentation of the Middle Way of the Two Truths as the concluding summary of the essential intent.
The reason for these two [chapters] is as follows:
from the preceding sections onward, the "disease of existence" has been refuted;
now, in this chapter, the "disease of emptiness" is successively refuted.
However, this notion of emptiness and existence obstructs the Buddha’s two truths;
one must first destroy these obstructions before the two truths can be clearly elucidated.
Furthermore, by first destroying emptiness and existence, one clarifies that which is neither empty nor existent.
This is precisely the meaning of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*).
It is only because [reality] is neither empty nor existent that one can then provisionally designate it as "empty" or "existent.
These provisional designations of emptiness and existence are intended to reveal the non-dual path that is neither empty nor existent; thus, the Middle Way of the two truths is elucidated.
Furthermore, because externalists may give rise to the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) when the preceding [section] refuted both emptiness and existence,
the two truths are subsequently explained to counteract that nihilistic mind.
Moreover, it was previously clarified that the four positions— emptiness, existence, and so forth— are ultimately non-existent.
This is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Next, it is explained that the existence of what is non-existent is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Therefore, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by relying on these two truths.
The Master of the Treatise also relies upon the two truths in his study of the Buddha's teachings.
If one speaks apart from the two truths, it is merely false and deceptive.
Therefore, he first elucidates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and subsequently elucidates the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
You should simply study the text thoroughly and not rely on the words of others.
However, the entire treatise comprises five general sections.
From the beginning of the treatise up to this point constitutes the first section, which refutes the positions established by external schools.
The first section of this chapter intends to refute the two preceding refutations.
Next, because it refutes other doctrines, the passage beginning with "Therefore, you are a refuter" clarifies the three sections concerning the failure to establish non-refutation.

The section beginning with "Next, there should be [the existence of] all phenomena because they exist in mutual dependence" expresses the meaning of the four sections refuting the externalist claim that the internal [subject] ultimately has something that exists.

The section beginning with "Next, if it were empty, there should not be any teaching" expresses the meaning of the five sections wherein the externalist falls into nihilism, failing to recognize the two truths.
These five sections are not merely for use within this treatise;
when contemplating all Buddha-dharma, they must be applied to whatever the six sense organs encounter and to all four modes of conduct, whether moving or still.
This is why these five sections exist.
One must grasp this with precision so as to be able to leave behind even the subtle signs of obstruction characteristic of bodhisattvas;
for if one gives rise to even a hair’s breadth of views regarding person, phenomena, birth-and-death, or nirvana, then one's practice of the Way is outside of the mind.
To be called a "non-Buddhist" (tīrthika) is precisely what constitutes a "proposition" (sthāpana).
Since the beginning of this treatise, we have refuted such propositions; therefore, it is called "refuting the proposition" (sthāpana-pratiṣedha).
This is precisely the meaning of the first section.
Next, it is said that there is a correct contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*) which refutes what has been established above;
that which was established above is what is to be refuted.
The correct contemplation of non-arising is that which can destroy [delusion].
To form such a conceptualization is to fall into the duality of subject and object,
giving rise to a mind of refutation and establishment.
Therefore, the second section clarifies that what is to be refuted—such as birth-and-death and nirvana—is fundamentally non-existent;
likewise, the means of refutation—the correct contemplation of non-arising—has never existed either.
Since both the refuter and the refuted arise only from conceptual attachment, there is the intended meaning of the second section.
The opponent further argues:
"If there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, then that which is to be refuted does not exist;
likewise, there is no correct contemplation of non-arising that can serve as the refuter."
This is neither right nor wrong, neither internal nor external.
To destroy all phenomena is to be a person of great false views.
Therefore, one who understands that all phenomena were never established in the first place has nothing to refute.
You arbitrarily claim that [the reason] is established, yet you arbitrarily claim that it is refuted;
because one who possesses internal faults is, conversely, a person who refutes the doctrine,
the third section thus introduces the sense of neither being unestablished nor being refuted.
The opponent further says:
If you claim that there is neither establishment nor refutation at all,
how can it be that there is no objection where there is no penetration, and no penetration where there is no objection?
Since there is nothing that is not difficult for them to penetrate, and nothing that they do not find difficult to penetrate,
there must surely be some subtle artistry; thus,
they will ultimately have something upon which to rely.
Therefore, the Master of the Treatise clarifies:
if there were even a single dharma that did not exist, its existence might be possible;
yet, in the end, there is not a single dharma that does not exist.
"How can there be even a single dharma that can be maintained?
This constitutes the purpose of the fourth section.
Furthermore, the opponent says:
If one says that not even a single hair’s breadth can be maintained,
yet not even a single hair’s breadth can be non-existent,
then how could the Buddhas of the three periods of time have preached the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the eighty thousand dharma-treasuries to teach and transform sentient beings?

Therefore, it is next explained that although there has never been anything that is neither existent nor non-existent, nor neither non-existent nor not non-existent, one speaks in accordance with worldly convention for the sake of sentient beings.
Thus, the fifth section clarifies the two truths.
Regarding the meaning of the five sections:
the first section belongs to the preceding nine categories;
the fifth belongs to the second sub-section within this category.
The remaining three sections are contained within the first part,
which constitutes three points.
This treatise is based on the ancient interpretations of Chang’an.
Formerly, when I was in Jiangzuo,
I often remarked that although the traditions of Guanyin and Heshang had been passed down, those who later attained realization did not study this treatise;
most of them were merely attached to superficial appearances.
Now, in order to counteract this fault, four sections are established.
The first section correctly refutes the two kinds of selflessness and the three kinds of non-nature.
As for the second section, the opponent then says:
The "Chapter on Emptiness" first refutes the three natures;
the "Chapter on Emptiness" then refutes the three non-natures.
If both the three natures and the three non-natures, as well as the two selves and the two non-selves, are all refuted, [then all conceptual constructs are eliminated].
This refers to those who destroy the Dharma and those who extinguish the Dharma of the Buddha;
therefore, the answer says:
"You perceive the existence of established dharmas, as well as the arising of dharmas and the extinction of dharmas."
"You are merely one who destroys the Dharma.
I have never established the Dharma, nor do I destroy the Dharma;
because I have neither produced the Dharma nor extinguished the Dharma, I am not one who destroys the Dharma."
The third section states:
"If you say that my position involves establishment and refutation, as well as arising and ceasing, and is therefore false;
whereas your own position lacks establishment and refutation, as well as arising and ceasing, and is therefore correct."
In that case, there would ultimately be something attained and something upon which to rely.
How then can it be said that there is no reliance and nothing attained?
Therefore, the answer is given:
"You say that you have attained something by relying on me;
yet I have never possessed even a single atom of a dharma upon which one could rely for attainment.
The fourth section says:
If one attains non-reliance by means of non-reliance,

why does the Sūtra state that from the Dharma-body flow forth the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the treasury of the eightfold path, which teach and transform sentient beings so that they may cultivate the causes for attaining Buddhahood?
Therefore, the answer was given:
"This is merely the Buddha’s speech conforming to worldly convention;
in the ultimate Way, there has never been a single word."
How much more so the eighty thousand treasuries of Dharma!
The *Xiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts during the Semblance Dharma Age) states:
"From his initial attainment of enlightenment until his parinirvāṇa..."
"I have never uttered a single word, nor have I delivered a single person across [to liberation].
Yet sentient beings themselves perceive me preaching the Dharma and saving others.
This was my response to the late masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* and others, employing the traditional interpretation of Chang'an.
Regarding the first two questions and answers, which clarify the refutation, there are two intended meanings.
First, it refutes the opponent’s claim that the Master uses emptiness to refute existence;
thus, it refutes the opponent’s refutation of emptiness.
Next, the question-and-answer refutes the opponent’s claim that the Master uses existence (*sat*) to refute all phenomena,
clarifying that there is no such refutation.
Furthermore, the initial question-and-answer refutes the opponent’s view by demonstrating that internal activity is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) dependent upon conditions.
Next, the question-and-answer refutes the external by means of the internal using conditions as a provisional refutation.
Furthermore, the first question-and-answer refutes the external by means of the internal using the correct to refute the false.
The subsequent question-and-answer refutes the external by means of the internal borrowing the false to refute the false.
Now, all that which can refute and all that is to be refuted do not transcend these three pairs.
Herein it is clarified that, in reality, there has never been such an object to be refuted,
nor has there ever been such a subject capable of refuting.
The first section consists of a preliminary question followed by a response.
The question contains two points.
The opponent says: "There must be various dharmas, because they refute existence."
This is the refutation of the refuter from the perspective of existence;
there are five points in total.
First, since there is a refuter, there must be something to be refuted.
Therefore, one should not say that all phenomena exist and are empty.
Second, you possess the capacity to refute and I possess that which is to be refuted;
both are existent. Since that which is to be refuted by me has already been refuted by your capacity to refute, [your position falls].
If your refutation is itself refuted,
then Deva is no different from the common people.
How can you claim that the external is the object to be refuted and the internal is the subject that refutes?
Third, both the refuter and the refuted are equally existent.
If the refuter were also to employ the refuted as a refuter,
then the internal would become the refuted and the external would become the refuter.
Fourth, both the refuter and the refuted are equally existent;
if both are equally the refuted,
then there can be no refuter.
Since there is no refuter, there is nothing to be refuted.
If this is so, then there is neither a refuter nor a refutation;
how, then, could there be contraction or extension?

this reconciles the preceding statement.
Furthermore, the essence of the Buddhas is the Way, which is neither speech nor non-speech.
Now, I speak in accordance with worldly convention.
What fault is there in speaking thus?
Although I speak in accordance with worldly convention, in reality, there is nothing spoken.
When was it ever said [otherwise]?
The commentary states: "That which is always taught in reliance upon the two truths" means that ordinary beings, because they take the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) to be real, call it a truth (*satya*).
The Sage realizes emptiness as reality, and therefore it is called a "truth" (*satya*).
Because these two are spoken of based on what is real, both explanations are true.
Question: Why is it necessary to clarify that they are spoken of based on what is real?
Answer: This is intended to prevent external objections.
Since it was previously stated that all phenomena are inexpressible, one might now object that they are nevertheless being spoken of.
This would then constitute false speech. Therefore,
it is clarified here that because both are spoken in accordance with reality, both statements are true and not false.
The outsider says: "According to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), there is nothing that is not real.
The outsider, being clever, already anticipates that the meanings of the two truths are contradictory;
for the true [truth] possesses three characteristics by which it may be considered a truth.
First, emptiness is the true reality, and is therefore called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
it can be apprehended as the truth.
Second, emptiness is real for the noble ones (*ārya*).
This, too, is a truth.
Since the three are called "real," they are truths because they are real.
The mundane has three meanings for which it should not be termed "truth" (*satya*):
first, because existence is illusory and false, it should not be called truth;
second, because it is real only for ordinary people, it is insufficient to be called truly real.
Among the three [truths], that which lacks reality cannot be called a "truth" (satya).
Therefore, it is said that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is not unreal;
for if the conventional were itself the truth, it would then enter into the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, if both were truths, then both would have to be real.
Moreover, just as one distinguishes between the real and the conventional, one should likewise distinguish between what is a truth and what is not a truth.
Furthermore, if the conventional were ultimately a truth, then the real would not be a truth.
Furthermore, one may directly challenge this by saying:
"If it is ultimate truth, it cannot be conventional; if it is conventional, it cannot be ultimate.
How then can you say that there exists conventional truth?"
The internal [opponent] says: "Because they are mutually dependent, like 'large' and 'small'; this answers the previous [point] regarding the meaning of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This can be explained through two meanings.
First, the ultimate (*paramārtha*) is exclusively truth; there is nothing that is not truth.
Second, the conventional is both a truth and not a truth.
It is called a truth because it is real for ordinary people;
it is not called a truth because it is not real for the noble ones.
Therefore, this conventional reality is both true and not true.
As for "large and small": it is like the shape of an apple; whether compared to a melon or a jujube, its size is real in each case.
Question: What object does the mango (nālikera) definitively illustrate?

Answer: A certain master of the Three Treatises (Sanlun shi) says that the mango illustrates the conventional and ultimate truths versus what is not true, while the melon and jujube illustrate the two conditions of the ordinary person and the sage.
Furthermore, it is said that the mango (*nālikera*) illustrates a single color while the melon and jujube illustrate two conditions.
Now, I maintain that both the wording and the meaning of this are incorrect;
the mango properly illustrates the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Just as the fruit of the *nālikera* is small compared to the melon,
yet its form is large compared to the jujube fruit;
the largeness of the jujube fruit’s form is a metaphor for the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) among the mundane.
The comparison of the melon fruit being small, likening the mundane to the sacred, is not the ultimate truth;
the meaning of the text is precisely thus,
and not a single word may be altered.
Question: Why is the example of the mango fruit not valid?
Answer: The opponent is correctly challenging that the conventional should not be a truth.
Now, in directly answering whether the conventional is true or not true, one cannot use the analogy of a single color. Question:
If a melon is compared to a gourd or a jujube, they are all real in terms of their relative sizes.
Originally, that which is real by its own nature is taken as the truth (*satya*).
If both the Great and the Small Vehicles were equally real, then both should be considered truths.
The answer is: the intention of the analogy is not so.
This is explained as before.
It correctly takes the conventional;
for ordinary people, it is indeed a truth.
That which is unreal for the noble ones is not a truth;
one does not speak of two realities by grasping at both truth and non-truth.
These two realities are used as a metaphor for the two truths.
Therefore, the text says:
"Conventional truth is real for worldly people,
but unreal for the noble ones."
Therefore, by means of the analogy of the large and the small, it cannot be explained otherwise.
Furthermore, that which is not real in the case of the noble ones is empty because it is unreal.
Regarding the statement that emptiness is the noble reality, this can also be said to mean that both of these are real, which is precisely the meaning of the two truths.
Question: The conventional is a truth for ordinary beings, but it is not a truth for the noble ones.
One might also say that it is "true" because it is real for the noble ones and thus a "truth" (satya),
whereas for ordinary people it is not real and therefore not a truth.
To this, the various masters reply:
This is one instance of the principle;
now it may be applied universally. In general, that which is real belongs to the noble, while that which is empty belongs to the ordinary.
The reality of the sage is the emptiness of the ordinary person;
the emptiness of the ordinary person is the reality of the sage, while the emptiness of the sage is the reality of the ordinary person.
These cases are not analogous when distinguished separately.
In the conventional, there is the sense of both the real and the unreal;
in the ultimate, there is only the real and no unreality.
This is because the conventional is inverted and insubstantial, and thus is not real.
It is merely a truth in the conventional sense;
it is a truth because it is the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Furthermore, it is designated as "the real" (satya).
Furthermore, because it is realized by the Noble Ones, it is exclusively truth and nothing but truth;
the text is precisely thus and cannot be interpreted otherwise.
Question: How do your two truths differ from those of others?
Answer: Regarding the two [truths] for the proponent of the treatise, a single form has never been either true or conventional.
Because there are two types of understanding—those of ordinary beings and those of sages—it constitutes the two truths.
According to others, however, there are two objective realms of truth and conventionality based on reasoning;
thus, it differs [from the former].
Furthermore, based on two conditions, two [aspects] are established.
Form has never been either dual or non-dual.
Such are the five propositions.
Nor has it ever been [perceived as] true or untrue;
these five phrases are likewise.
It is asked: in common parlance, the mundane is called "truth."
What kind of ordinary person is this?
The answer is: this text is a general statement of conceptualization.
Worldly ordinary persons [conceptually] assert the existence of jars, clothes, the earth, and pillars.
It is called a "truth" (*satya*) because this thing actually exists.
A question is raised: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that ordinary beings do not know conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If one knows this, then one is a srotāpanna.
Why, then, do you say that ordinary persons possess conventional truth?
Answer: The present text discusses this in terms of two perspectives.
That which is real with respect to ordinary beings is therefore called a "truth" (satya).
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"What is known by worldly people is called worldly truth."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Those who do not know" means they do not know that this existence is an existence of emptiness; thus, they do not know the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The Sage, having realized that existence is non-existent, knows that which is non-existent as existent.
Therefore, the Sage understands the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Furthermore, there are four kinds of meanings.
The first is the meaning of the two truths (satyadvaya).
1. The meaning of teaching the Dharma based on the two truths; 2.
Explaining the meaning of the two truths; 3.
The meaning of teaching by means of the two truths.
Regarding the meaning of the two truths:
as previously stated, that which is real for ordinary beings is the truth;
that which is emptiness is real for the noble ones and is thus the truth.
Regarding the teaching based on the two truths:
if one says that emptiness is real, it is said in reliance upon the ultimate truth;
if one says that existence is real, it is said in reliance upon the conventional truth.
Regarding the teaching of the two truths:
one teaches the two truths by relying upon the two truths.
As for the teaching of the two truths:
Briefly stated, to speak of the ineffable is called the teaching of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),

while to speak of the expressible is called the teaching of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Thus, within the conventional truth, one may speak of the conventional truth, and one may speak of the ultimate truth.
Ultimate truth is inexpressible;
as stated in the "Chapter on the Four Truths" of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, verbal expression belongs to the conventional.
Nevertheless, although the conventional involves speech, it is eternally transcendent.
Therefore, although conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) speaks, it is in fact non-speaking;
although ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is without speaking, it does not obstruct speaking.
Thus, one attains the speaking of ultimate truth.
Question: What does this mean?
Answer: Not only is the truth that is expressed beyond words, but the words that express that truth are themselves eternally transcendent of speech.
Therefore, this speaking is precisely non-speaking;
having attained this, it is precisely that speaking is non-speaking.
Since it is non-speaking, how could it not be precisely speaking?
Therefore, it can be said that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is attained.
If this is so, one would fully attain all four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi): both being stated and not being stated, both being mutually stated and not being mutually stated.
The opponent asks: "Knowing this fault, what benefit is gained?"
The treatise consists of three parts.
Two parts have already been concluded;
now follows the third, which turns away from error and enters into correctness, requesting spiritual benefit.
According to the text, there are two parts:
the first clarifies the attainment of benefit,
and the second distinguishes the characteristics of that benefit.
Now, the externalist asks:
"From the initial relinquishing of sin and merit, through the ultimate destruction of emptiness, the horizontal crushing of the myriad dharmas, and the vertical exhaustion of the five propositions—
what benefit is there for one who acts with such knowledge?"
The internal [proponent] says: "Thus, the relinquishing of the self is what constitutes attaining liberation; this is the correct answer that benefits [the seeker].
Question: Since everything above has been horizontally exhausted and vertically refuted such that not a single thing remains, why do you specifically speak only of "relinquishing the self"?
Answer: Because the non-Buddhists wish to cause one to abandon the self in order to attain liberation, they speak specifically of abandoning the self.
Furthermore, the three types of emptiness were explained above:
first, the emptiness of the self; second, the emptiness of phenomena; and third, the emptiness of emptiness.
I am the first among them; by mentioning the first, the subsequent ones are included.
Furthermore, all non-Buddhists take the self (ātman) as their primary tenet.
Now, the primary examples are cited as the standard.
Furthermore, the view of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi) subsumes the sixty-two views;
this cites the root to exemplify the branches.
Furthermore, because I am the subject of contemplation and claim that "I" can perform the contemplation of the three emptinesses,
I specifically clarify the relinquishing of this "self."
Every time the Great Master Xinghuang ascended the high seat, he would always say:
"I do not fear the afflictions; I only fear the 'self'.
The reason for this was as follows:
He said: "Because one must sever afflictions yet leave sentient beings behind, causing them to become Buddhas,
and because this vision is difficult to eliminate, sentient beings are to be feared."
Master Xinghuang borrowed the words of Li Er (Laozi) and said:
for those who study, there is increase;
for those who cultivate the Way, there is decrease.
Diminish it again and again until there is ultimately no diminishing.
Both internal and external are extinguished, and both object and contemplation are stilled.
Thus one attains the Way. The opponent asks:
"On what basis do you say that one attains liberation? This is the second section, distinguishing the characteristics of the benefits attained.
The opponent maintains that one must truly attain the Way.
Why is it said that liberation is merely a provisional designation?
For instance, in the Hīnayāna, one truly severs the afflictions of views and thoughts and truly attains liberation;
in the Mahāyāna, one truly severs the five stages of dwelling and the two obstacles and truly attains liberation.
Now it is the same with the outsiders.
The internal [teaching] says: "Because it is ultimately pure.
This is the root verse.
As for the statement that "now there is none," it is because the text has been omitted;
it is neither liberated nor bound, and there is nothing it cannot do.
I do not know how to designate it.
Because it is forcibly designated as "liberation," it is merely called "attaining liberation.
End of the lower fascicle of the *Śata-śāstra-vyākhyā*.
